title: Writing Your First Program: Hello, World!
summary: Learn how to create, run, and understand the classic Hello, World! program. This lesson introduces basic syntax, compilation, and execution steps.

sections.heading: What is a Hello, World! Program?
sections.body:
The Hello, World! program is the simplest code you can write in any language. It displays the text "Hello, World!" on the screen, showing that the development environment works.

It is often the first step for beginners because it proves that you can write, compile, and run a program successfully.

sections.heading: Writing the Code
sections.body:
Open your IDE and create a new file named hello.c (or hello.py for Python). Type the following lines exactly as shown. The program consists of a main function, a print statement, and a return statement.

Make sure to save the file before you try to run it.

sections.heading: Compiling and Running
sections.body:
To turn the source code into an executable, you must compile it. In a terminal, type `gcc hello.c -o hello` and press Enter. If there are no errors, an executable named hello will appear.

Run the program by typing `./hello`. You should see the message "Hello, World!" printed on the screen.

sections.heading: Understanding the Output
sections.body:
The text you see is produced by the `printf` function, which sends characters to the standard output (your screen). The "\n" at the end adds a new line so the cursor moves to the next line after printing.

If you change the text inside the quotes, the program will display whatever you write, letting you experiment with different messages.

quiz.why: `printf` sends formatted text to the standard output.

quiz.q: Which command compiles a C program named hello.c?
quiz.why: `gcc hello.c -o hello` tells the GNU compiler to create an executable called hello.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the `return 0;` line in the main function?
options: It ends the program and signals success
quiz.why: Returning 0 tells the operating system that the program finished without errors.

quiz.q: If you change the text inside the quotes to "Good morning!", what will the program display?
quiz.why: The string inside the quotes is what `printf` outputs.
